questions.question: Explain the role of macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) in / supporting energy production during exercise
questions.solution_html:
• supporting energy production during exercise.
  • Carbohydrates: The primary high-intensity fuel source. Stored as glycogen in
  • muscles and liver; metabolized rapidly through anaerobic and aerobic
  • pathways.
  • Fats: The primary fuel source for low-to-moderate intensity, long-duration
  • exercise. Highly dense energy storage, but requires abundant oxygen to
  • convert into usable ATP.
  • Proteins: Primarily used for structural tissue repair and enzyme synthesis.
  • Contributes minimally to energy production (around 5% to 10%) unless
  • carbohydrate stores are severely depleted.

questions.question: Describe how knowledge of energy systems can help athletes plan training
questions.solution_html:
• optimize performance, and delay fatigue during exercise.
  • The Three Key Energy Systems
  • ATP-PCr System (Phosphagen): Anaerobic, ultra-short duration (0-10s), high
  • power output (e.g., 100m sprint).
  • Glycolytic System (Lactic Acid): Anaerobic, short-to-medium duration (10s-2
  • mins), yields lactic acid/hydrogen ions as byproducts.
  • Oxidative System (Aerobic): Requires oxygen, long duration (over 2 mins)
  • uses fats and carbohydrates, high total yield but slow delivery.
  • Training Design: Allows targeted conditioning. A weightlifter trains the ATP
  • PCr pathway with long recovery intervals, while an 800m runner develops
  • anaerobic threshold buffering.
  • Optimizing Performance: Teaches athletes when to push and when to coast
  • based on which fuel tank they are drawing from.
  • Delaying Fatigue: Aerobic training boosts mitochondrial density, helping
  • clear lactic acid faster and pushing the anaerobic threshold further down
  • the timeline.

questions.question: Explain the three classes of levers in the human body with examples for / . Discuss how understanding lever mechanics helps in analyzing CO5] movement efficiency
questions.solution_html:
• each. Discuss how understanding lever mechanics helps in analyzing movement
  • efficiency.
  • Lever Principles: Identify the components: Fulcrum (F) (joint), Effort (E)
  • (muscle contraction force), and Resistance/Load (R) (weight of body
  • segment or external object).
  • The Three Lever Classes
  • First-Class Lever (E-F-R): The fulcrum sits in the middle. Example: Extension
  • of the neck (Atlanto-occipital joint).
  • Second-Class Lever (F-R-E): The resistance sits in the middle. Offers high
  • mechanical advantage (magnifies force). Example: Plantar flexion standing
  • on tiptoes (metatarsophalangeal joint).
  • Third-Class Lever (F-E-R): The effort sits in the middle. Most common lever
  • in the body. Sacrifices force production for speed and range of motion.
  • Example: Biceps curl at the elbow joint.
  • Movement Efficiency Analysis
  • Explains why shifting an external load closer to a joint (shortening the
  • resistance arm) reduces the effort required by muscles.
  • Helps calculate the structural load placed on tendons, explaining why third
  • class setups demand massive internal muscular force to overcome small
  • external loads.
